newsitem.title: USA: China sells Iran missile tech, chemicals - report.
newsitem.headline: China sells Iran missile tech, chemicals - report.

text.p: China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tons of chemicals used to produce nerve agents, the Washington Times reported on Thursday, citing the Central Intelligence Agency.

In an article ahead of a weekend meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the newspaper said the reported transfer of missile-guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's commitment to an international pact on curbing such sales.

In addition, some of the reported arms-technology transfers may violate a 1992 U.S. law that requires sanctions to be imposed on any nation exporting destabilising conventional weapons to Iran or Iraq, the newspaper said.

State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said the United States had concerns about reports of Chinese missile cooperation with Iran and sales to Tehran of "dual-use" chemicals -- that can be used to make poison gas.

But Davies told a news briefing: "We believe at this stage that, in fact, the Chinese are operating within the assurances they have given us" on adherence to U.S. laws and international agreements on arms exports. "We've not seen any reason to question their behaviour," he said.

Citing intelligence considerations, Davies declined to comment on the details of the Washington Times report, which appeared as Secretary of State Warren Christopher ended two days of talks in China that included proliferation issues.

Quoting what it called a top-secret October 2 CIA report titled "Arms Transfers to State Sponsors of Terrorism," the Washington Times said the China Precision Engineering Department had agreed in August to sell gyroscopes and other high-technology devices to Iran that could be used to build and test missile guidance components.

It also delivered in the summer nearly 400 metric tons of chemicals, including carbon sulfide, used to make nerve gas, and another chemical used in producing riot-control agents and tear gas, the paper quoted the CIA report as saying.
The CIA also reported the shipment of air defence gear and about 5,000 metric tons of other military equipment, possibly to upgrade Iran's Chinese-made anti-ship missiles, the newspaper said.

In Shanghai on Thursday, Christopher praised what he called Chinese steps to improve civil rights and implored Beijing to seize an opportunity to build a new era of cooperation with the United States.
"As nuclear powers, permanent members of the U.N. Security Council and two of the world's biggest economies, we must lead" to promote global peace and prosperity, Christopher said.

The Clinton administration, eager to put ties with China on a more positive footing, has decided against imposing sanctions this year in several possible breaches of arms control pacts, including the sale of nuclear technology to Pakistan. Chinese leaders claimed they were unaware of the sale.
